title.rendered: Steampunk Accessories for Men: The Complete 2026 Checklist (Budget to Premium)

content.rendered:
Steampunk accessories for men are what turn a plain waistcoat-and-trousers combo into a character people ask to photograph. The good news: the base look is built on real Victorian menswear — which is why it works — and you can assemble a convincing kit for under $50 or go as deep as your wallet allows. This checklist covers every accessory category, what it costs in 2026, and the mistakes that make outfits read “Halloween” instead of “inventor.”

The 8 accessory categories that matter

Men’s steampunk is Victorian workwear plus machine-age details. After sorting through what top costume shops and veterans actually stock and recommend, these are the categories that do the work:

  1. Goggles — the single most recognizable steampunk item. Worn on eyes, forehead or hat brim.
  2. Hat — top hat, bowler/derby, flat-top gambler hat for a Western look, or a newsboy/deerstalker cap for a working-class inventor. A leather or brass hat band is the cheapest upgrade that reads “steampunk.”
  3. Pocket watch — ideally on a vest chain (an “Albert chain”). It anchors the Victorian silhouette.
  4. Gloves — fingerless leather gloves or lace-cuff gloves for dressier looks.
  5. Belt & holster — a wide leather utility belt or holster rig carries goggles, tools or a prop sidearm.
  6. Bag — leather satchel, medical bag or canvas rucksack. Practical at conventions: it holds your stuff in character.
  7. Jewelry — cufflinks, rings and lapel pins (often gear- or clockwork-shaped).
  8. Footwear details — leather spats or boot covers over plain boots.

What it costs: three honest budget tiers

Retail prices (checked October 2026 against US costume retailers) fall into rough tiers:

Tier Budget What you get
Starter $20–50 Goggles, one hat with a leather band, fingerless gloves. Costume-shop goggles run $10–25; boots at big costume retailers start around $39.99.
Serious $50–120 Pocket watch with vest chain, holster belt, satchel, quality leather gloves, decorated hat.
Collector $120+ Real antique pocket watches (working Victorian pieces start around $100 on auction sites), custom leatherwork, brass goggles with lighting mods.

The cheapest wins first

If you upgrade in order, buy these first: (1) goggles, (2) hat + hat band, (3) gloves. Those three alone make a shirt-and-waistcoat outfit photograph as steampunk. Everything else is detail.

D-I-Y or buy?

Goggles are the classic DIY project — a pair of welding goggles, craft gears and a leather strap gets you a custom pair in an afternoon. We compare the DIY and buy routes in detail in our DIY vs. buy goggles guide, and walk through the full build in DIY steampunk goggles. Bags, belts and watches are usually better bought: real leather goods at thrift stores often beat costume-shop quality at lower prices.

Three mistakes that cheapen the look

  • Plastic everything. Steampunk reads as metal, leather and wood. If an accessory is shiny plastic, spray-paint it brass/bronze or leave it out.
  • Too many gears. Gears glued on everything is the “beginner tell.” One or two gear accents (hat, lapel) beats ten.
  • Modern watches and phones on the belt. A pocket watch on a chain costs little and fixes the silhouette’s biggest gap.

Convention note: prop weapons

Prop pistols and rifles complete an airship-captain look, but every convention has its own prop-weapon rules — most require orange tips and peace-bonding, and some ban realistic replicas outright. Check the event’s policy before bringing anything weapon-shaped.

FAQ

What accessories do men need for steampunk at minimum?

Goggles and a hat with a leather or brass band. With a white shirt, waistcoat and trousers, that’s a complete, recognizable outfit for around $30–50.

Can steampunk accessories work with normal clothes?

Yes — that’s the “casual steampunk” route. A bowler hat, fingerless gloves and a pocket watch over everyday clothes is a common low-effort entry. See our casual steampunk outfits guide.

Where’s the best place to buy men’s steampunk accessories?

Costume retailers for cheap starters ($10–40 per item), specialty merchants like Museum Replicas for mid-range leather and brass, and auction/thrift sites for real Victorian pieces. Our shop stocks goggles and gear shipped from vetted suppliers.

The takeaway

Build from the silhouette out: goggles, hat, gloves, then watch and belt. Spend $20–50 to start, upgrade leather and metal as you go, and skip the plastic. Want the full head-to-toe plan? Start with our steampunk costume ideas and costume hub.

Every piece named here is in the shop: start with goggles, hats and accessories, or the Gothic & Victorian tailoring.

title.rendered: What Is Dieselpunk? A Guide to the Diesel & Deco Aesthetic

content.rendered:
Dieselpunk is a retro-futuristic aesthetic built on the look of the 1920s to the 1950s: art deco skyscrapers, streamlined machines, airships, noir shadows and the roar of diesel engines. Where steampunk imagines a future powered by Victorian steam and brass, dieselpunk imagines one powered by oil, chrome and industrial ambition, darker, faster and louder.

This guide covers where the style comes from, how it differs from steampunk, its key visual elements, and how to bring it into your wardrobe and walls.

Dieselpunk in one sentence

If steampunk asks "what if the Victorians had built the future?", dieselpunk asks "what if the machine age between the World Wars never ended?"

Where dieselpunk comes from

The term appeared in the early 2000s, borrowing the "-punk" ending from cyberpunk and steampunk. The look itself is much older. It draws on the real design language of the interwar years:

  • Art deco architecture and graphics: stepped skyscrapers, sunbursts, bold geometric lettering
  • Streamline moderne: smooth, teardrop-shaped trains, cars and radios designed to look fast even standing still
  • The age of airships and early aviation: zeppelins, flying boats and leather flight jackets
  • Pulp magazines and film noir: rocket heroes, trench coats, rain-soaked city streets
  • Industrial propaganda posters: heroic workers, massive machines, dramatic upward angles

Classic films such as Metropolis (1927) shaped the visual vocabulary early on, and later films like The Rocketeer (1991) and Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow (2004) helped define dieselpunk for modern audiences.

Dieselpunk vs. steampunk

Steampunk Dieselpunk
Era Victorian, roughly 1830s-1900s Interwar to post-war, roughly 1920s-1950s
Power Steam, clockwork, gears Diesel, oil, electricity, early jet and rocket
Materials Brass, copper, leather, wood Chrome, steel, riveted plate, bakelite
Shapes Ornate, curly, Victorian Geometric, streamlined, art deco
Mood Curious, adventurous, optimistic Gritty, noir, industrial
Colours Brass, sepia, deep reds and browns Gunmetal, black, gold, oxblood, olive drab

Many fans enjoy both. They share the same idea, an alternative history where technology took a different turn, and sit side by side in the wider family of retro-futurism alongside atompunk and decopunk.

The two faces of dieselpunk

Dieselpunk tends to split into two moods:

Decopunk is the glamorous side: gold and black art deco, polished chrome, grand hotels, cocktail lounges and elegant streamlined trains. Think luxury and optimism.

The grittier side leans into wartime and industry: rivets, oil stains, flight goggles, aviator jackets, massive war machines and noir detective stories.

Key visual elements

If you want to recognise or create dieselpunk design, look for:

  1. Art deco geometry: sunbursts, chevrons, stepped forms and symmetrical frames
  2. Streamlining: long horizontal speed lines and rounded, aerodynamic shapes
  3. Riveted metal and chrome: industrial surfaces with visible construction
  4. Aviation: biplanes, airships, rocket packs and flight gear
  5. Bold poster typography: tall condensed lettering in the style of 1930s travel and industry posters
  6. Strong contrast lighting: deep noir shadows and dramatic beams of light

How to wear dieselpunk

Dieselpunk fashion is easier to wear every day than many costume styles, because it builds on real vintage clothing:

  • For a 1930s-40s base: high-waisted trousers, braces, waistcoats, pencil skirts and button-up shirts
  • Outerwear: leather aviator or bomber jackets, trench coats and long wool coats
  • Accessories: flight goggles, leather gloves, newsboy caps, fedoras and art deco jewellery
  • Details: brass or chrome buttons, utility belts and wristwatches with bold industrial dials

A simple graphic tee with an art deco or machine-age print under a leather jacket is the easiest everyday way into the style.

Dieselpunk at home

On the walls, dieselpunk looks best as art deco-style posters: airships over stepped city skylines, streamlined locomotives, rocket heroes and industrial landscapes in a limited palette of black, gold and cream. Pair them with black frames, warm lighting and a little chrome or brass.

Dieselpunk at Steamgears

At Steamgears, dieselpunk lives in our Diesel & Deco collection, a sister line to our steampunk and Gaslight designs, coming in early 2027. It will start with a small series of art deco-inspired prints.

Until then, explore the rest of our retro-futurist world, from the Victorian gothic of the Clockwork Herbarium to classic steampunk gear.

Materials, silhouettes and colour

The two eras had different industrial capabilities, and the costume materials follow. Steampunk is warm and handmade: mahogany, sepia, antique brass, burnished copper, dark brown leather, forest green, with visible mechanisms — cut gears, copper piping, pressure gauges, blown glass. Dieselpunk is cold and mass-produced: battleship grey, charcoal, matte black, olive drab, chrome, stark white, with stamp-formed steel, cast iron, riveted aluminium, rubber tubing, Bakelite and oilskin.

The silhouettes split the same way. Steampunk borrows the nineteenth century — tailcoats, waistcoats, corsetry, cravats, top hats — and is ornamental and bespoke. Dieselpunk borrows the 1930s and 1940s — double-breasted trench coats, bomber jackets, mechanic coveralls, pencil skirts, fedoras — and is utilitarian and uniform-like.

Converting a steampunk costume to dieselpunk

If you already own steampunk kit, four swaps move it a century forward:

  1. Headwear: trade the top hat for a leather pilot cap or a wool newsboy cap.
  2. Base layer: swap lace blouses and brocade vests for heavy flannel, chambray work shirts, or olive wool trousers.
  3. Eye protection: keep wearing goggles, but choose stamped aluminium or chrome frames with rubber gaskets instead of round brass and magnifying loupes.
  4. Gear: replace brass rayguns with utilitarian props — analogue dials, spark plugs, Bakelite switches.

The most common mistake is gluing loose, non-functional gears onto modern clothing. Dieselpunk reads as machinery that was actually built, so every part should look like it does something.

Trenchpunk: the hybrid

You can combine the two, provided the result looks like a clear technological evolution rather than a costume of two halves. The border zone around the First World War is sometimes called trenchpunk. Put late-Victorian tailoring under functional field gear: a tweed waistcoat beneath a heavy canvas trench coat, or brass mechanisms sealed inside a painted steel chassis. The rule is that the machine should look updated during rapid wartime industrialisation.

Frequently asked questions

Is dieselpunk the same as steampunk?
No. Both are retro-futuristic, but steampunk is based on the Victorian era and steam power, while dieselpunk is based on the 1920s-1950s and diesel, oil and electricity.

What is the difference between dieselpunk and decopunk?
Decopunk is usually seen as the glamorous, art deco-focused side of dieselpunk, with more gold, chrome and elegance, and less grit.

What colours are dieselpunk?
Black, gunmetal, chrome, gold and cream, often with oxblood red or olive drab as accents.

Is dieselpunk the same as atompunk?
No. Atompunk picks up roughly where dieselpunk ends, inspired by the 1950s and 60s atomic and space age: rockets, rayguns, fins and bright optimistic colours.

More of a brass-and-clockwork person? Read steampunk vs dieselpunk, then browse the Dark Academia and Steampunk Capsule collections.

title.rendered: The Best Steampunk Books: A Reading Guide for Every Kind of Reader

content.rendered:
The best steampunk books to start with are The Difference Engine, Boneshaker, Leviathan, Soulless and Mortal Engines. Between them they cover the main flavours of the genre: alternate history, adventure, young adult, comedy of manners and post-apocalyptic. Below is a reading guide with a short note on each book, who it suits, and where the genre came from.

Quick picks

If you want… Read
The book that shaped the genre The Difference Engine (1990)
Airships, zombies and the American frontier Boneshaker (2009)
A young adult adventure with illustrations Leviathan (2009)
Wit, tea and werewolves Soulless (2009)
Giant moving cities Mortal Engines (2001)
Victorian time travel and dark magic The Anubis Gates (1983)
A strange, dense, unforgettable city Perdido Street Station (2000)

Where the word "steampunk" came from

The word was coined by author K. W. Jeter in a 1987 letter to the science fiction magazine Locus. He used it half-jokingly to describe the Victorian-set fantasies that he, Tim Powers and James Blaylock were writing at the time, as a playful twist on "cyberpunk". The name stuck, and the genre grew from there.

The classics that started it

The Anubis Gates — Tim Powers (1983)

A modern scholar travels back to London in 1810 and becomes trapped there among sorcerers, beggar guilds and Egyptian magic. Fast, inventive and full of twists. One of the founding books of the genre.

Morlock Night — K. W. Jeter (1979)

A sequel of sorts to H. G. Wells’s The Time Machine, in which the Morlocks invade Victorian London. Short, strange and historically important.

Homunculus — James P. Blaylock (1986)

An eccentric Victorian adventure with airships, scientists and a mysterious creature. Gentler and funnier than many of its successors.

The Difference Engine — William Gibson & Bruce Sterling (1990)

What if Charles Babbage’s mechanical computer had actually been built in the 1800s? Two founders of cyberpunk imagine an information age that arrived a century early. Demanding but rewarding, and the book many people see as the genre’s cornerstone.

Modern favourites

Boneshaker — Cherie Priest (2009)

In an alternate 1880s Seattle, a drilling machine has released a toxic gas that turns people into the walking dead, and the city has been walled off. A mother goes inside to find her son. Airships, gas masks and frontier grit; the first book in the Clockwork Century series.

Leviathan — Scott Westerfeld (2009)

An alternate First World War between the "Clankers", who build walking war machines, and the "Darwinists", who engineer living creatures, including an airship that is a giant flying whale. Written for young adults, beautifully illustrated, and a great entry point for any age.

Soulless — Gail Carriger (2009)

Alexia Tarabotti has no soul, which makes her very inconvenient for the vampires and werewolves of Victorian London society. A witty comedy of manners with parasols, dirigibles and plenty of tea. The first of the Parasol Protectorate series.

Mortal Engines — Philip Reeve (2001)

In a far future, whole cities roll across the land on giant wheels and devour smaller towns for fuel. Technically post-apocalyptic, but its traction cities, airships and scavenged machinery make it a favourite with steampunk readers.

Perdido Street Station — China Miéville (2000)

Set in the sprawling, grimy city of New Crobuzon, where a renegade scientist accidentally unleashes monstrous moths that feed on dreams. More "New Weird" than pure steampunk, but its industrial magic and decaying grandeur have inspired a generation of steampunk artists.

Clockwork Angel — Cassandra Clare (2010)

Victorian London, a young woman with a hidden power, and an army of clockwork automatons. A popular young adult gateway into the genre.

The Victorian roots

Steampunk owes a great deal to two writers who imagined the future from inside the 19th century:

  • Jules Verne: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea (1870) gave us Captain Nemo and the submarine Nautilus, still one of the most copied designs in steampunk art.
  • H. G. Wells: The Time Machine (1895) and The War of the Worlds (1898) set the template for Victorian science fiction.

Reading one of each is the best way to understand where the aesthetic comes from.

Where to start

  • New to the genre: Leviathan or Boneshaker
  • Want something funny: Soulless
  • Want the history: The Anubis Gates, then The Difference Engine
  • Want something darker and stranger: Perdido Street Station

A story of our own

If you enjoy steampunk fiction, read our free short story, The Clockwork Herbarium, about a Victorian illustrator who rebuilds her father’s dying plant collection in brass. It is the story behind our Clockwork Herbarium series of tees, prints and phone cases.

Frequently asked questions

What was the first steampunk book?
There is no single first book, but Morlock Night (1979), The Anubis Gates (1983) and Homunculus (1986) are usually named as the founding novels. The word itself was coined by K. W. Jeter in 1987.

What is the best steampunk book for beginners?
Leviathan by Scott Westerfeld and Boneshaker by Cherie Priest are both easy to get into and full of classic steampunk imagery.

Is steampunk only for young adults?
No. There are steampunk books for every age, from young adult adventures like Leviathan to complex adult novels like The Difference Engine.

Are Jules Verne and H. G. Wells steampunk?
Not strictly, because they were writing about their own present and near future. But their work is the main inspiration for the genre, and they are often called proto-steampunk.

title.rendered: What Is Gaslamp Fantasy? Victorian Magic, Explained

content.rendered:
Gaslamp fantasy is fantasy set in a Victorian or Edwardian world, where magic, ghosts and the supernatural live alongside gaslit streets, drawing rooms and old libraries. Where steampunk is about the machines, gaslamp fantasy is about the atmosphere: fog, candlelight, secrets and the strange things hidden behind good manners.

This guide explains what gaslamp fantasy is, how it differs from steampunk and gothic fiction, and how to bring the look into your home and wardrobe.

Gaslamp fantasy in one sentence

If steampunk asks "what if the Victorians had built impossible machines?", gaslamp fantasy asks "what if Victorian London had real magic hiding in it?"

Where the term comes from

The phrase was popularised by Phil and Kaja Foglio, the creators of the comic Girl Genius, who used it to describe their work instead of "steampunk". It has since become the common name for a whole family of Victorian and Edwardian fantasy, including stories written long before the label existed.

Gaslamp fantasy vs. steampunk vs. gothic

Gaslamp fantasy Steampunk Gothic
Heart of the story Magic, the supernatural, manners Technology and invention Fear, decay, the past
Era Victorian and Edwardian Mostly Victorian Often 18th-19th century
Typical setting Gaslit cities, libraries, drawing rooms Airships, workshops, factories Ruined castles, old houses
Mood Mysterious, elegant, eerie Adventurous, inventive Dark, dramatic, melancholy
Key objects Spellbooks, specimen jars, candles, tarot Gears, goggles, gauges Crypts, portraits, ravens

The three overlap a lot. A story about a clockmaker who builds a mechanical heart for a ghost would sit happily in all three.

Books to start with

  • Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell (Susanna Clarke, 2004): two rival magicians bring English magic back during the Napoleonic Wars. Often called the defining modern gaslamp fantasy.
  • Sorcery & Cecelia (Patricia C. Wrede and Caroline Stevermer, 1988): a magical Regency adventure told through letters between two cousins.
  • The Prestige (Christopher Priest, 1995): two rival Victorian stage magicians and a secret that blurs the line between illusion and science.
  • Girl Genius (Phil and Kaja Foglio): the comic that gave the genre its name.

For more, see our guide to the best steampunk books, many of which share the same gaslit world.

The gaslamp look

Gaslamp fantasy has a very recognisable visual style:

  1. Low, warm light: candles, oil lamps and gas lamps against deep shadow
  2. Natural history and curiosities: pressed flowers, pinned moths, specimen jars, skulls and shells
  3. Old paper and engraving: copperplate illustrations, maps, botanical plates and handwritten labels
  4. Dark, rich colours: black, deep green, oxblood, aged cream and antique brass
  5. The occult and the mysterious: tarot cards, ravens, keys, locked books and apothecary bottles

Gaslamp fantasy at home

The easiest way to bring the style home is through the walls. Vintage botanical prints and natural history engravings in sepia and brass, framed in black, instantly give a room a gaslit library feel. Add warm lighting, dark wood, a few old books and a brass object or two.

It sits very close to dark academia decor, and the two mix naturally.

How to wear it

  • Base: dark trousers or long skirts, high-collared blouses and shirts, waistcoats
  • Outerwear: long dark coats, capes and velvet jackets
  • Details: cameo brooches, pocket watches, lace, small brass jewelry
  • Everyday: a black tee with a Victorian engraving print under a dark coat is the simplest way into the look

Gaslamp fantasy at Steamgears

At Steamgears, gaslamp fantasy lives in our Gaslight collection. Its first series, The Clockwork Herbarium, imagines a lost Victorian field journal in which every specimen was rebuilt in brass: a clockwork rose, a luna moth with gear wings, a raven guarding a pocket watch and a nightshade apothecary bottle with a clockwork heart. Each design is available as a tee, an art print and a phone case.

Read the story behind it in our free short story, The Clockwork Herbarium.

Frequently asked questions

Is gaslamp fantasy the same as steampunk?
No. Steampunk focuses on technology and invention, while gaslamp fantasy focuses on magic and the supernatural in a Victorian or Edwardian setting. They often overlap.

Is gaslamp fantasy the same as gothic fiction?
Not quite. Gothic fiction centres on fear, decay and dark secrets. Gaslamp fantasy shares the setting and mood but is often more adventurous or whimsical.

What is an example of gaslamp fantasy?
Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell by Susanna Clarke is the best-known modern example.

What colours suit gaslamp fantasy decor?
Black, deep green, oxblood red, aged cream and antique brass, with warm low lighting.

Want the look rather than the reading list? The Dark Academia collection carries the same cabinet-of-curiosities mood in tees, hoodies and prints.

title.rendered: The Last Flight of the Meridian: A Dieselpunk Short Story

content.rendered:
An original short story from the Diesel & Deco collection. About an eight-minute read.

Want the look? The vintage maritime prints and the dark clockwork pieces are built on the same interwar palette — chrome, oxblood and cream.

I. The Last Ticket

In the spring of 1937, the airship Meridian was scheduled to make her final flight.

Everyone in the city of Halcyon knew it. The newspapers had printed her photograph on the front page for a week: four hundred feet of silver skin, her nose pointed at the great stepped towers of the Aurelia Building, the city’s lights reflected along her flanks like a string of pearls. END OF AN ERA, the headlines said. The new diesel liners crossed the ocean in half the time. The airlines had no use for a grand old lady who took three days to do anything.

Captain Rosalind Mercer had flown her for eleven years. She did not read the newspapers.

On the morning of the last flight, she stood at the foot of the mooring tower with her cap under her arm and watched the ground crew load the final mail sacks. The passenger list was short. Most of the city’s wealthy had already moved on to the fast liners; the ones who came today came for the photographs.

Which was why she noticed the girl.

She was perhaps twelve, in a coat two sizes too big, standing very still at the edge of the crowd and staring up at the Meridian as though it were the only thing in the world. She had no ticket. She had no parents with her. She had, Rosalind noted, a canvas bag over one shoulder and the particular stillness of someone working up courage.

"She’s going to try it," said Mr. Okafor, the chief engineer, at Rosalind’s elbow.

"I know."

"Shall I call the porter?"

Rosalind watched the girl a moment longer. "No," she said. "Let’s see how good she is."

II. The Stowaway

She was very good.

The Meridian was three hours out over the bay, the city a glittering model behind them, when Mr. Okafor knocked on the door of the control car and stood aside to reveal the girl, smudged with engine grease from crown to boots.

"Found her in the number two engine gondola," he said. "She’d tightened a loose fuel coupling before I got there. Did it properly, too."

The girl lifted her chin. "It was dripping."

"What’s your name?" Rosalind asked.

"Iris Kemp."

"And what are you doing on my ship, Iris Kemp?"

The girl hesitated, then told the truth all at once, the way children do when they have rehearsed a lie and abandoned it. Her father had built engines for the Meridian at the yards on the east river. He had talked about her every night at supper: the lift cells, the diesel engines in their gondolas, the way she turned in the wind like something alive. He had died in the winter. And this morning, when the newspapers said it was the last flight, Iris had decided that one of them, at least, would ride in her.

Nobody said anything for a while. The engines droned. Through the long windows, the evening sun turned the cloud tops to copper.

"Mr. Okafor," Rosalind said at last. "Does the number two gondola still need an engineer’s mate?"

"It does, Captain. Very much."

"Then she can work her passage."

III. The Storm

The storm caught them over the open sea on the second night.

It came up from the south faster than the forecasts had promised: a black wall of cloud, lightning walking along its edge. The Meridian shuddered as the first gusts hit her. Somewhere above the control car, a girder groaned.

"We can’t climb over it," said the navigator. "Not at this weight."

"Then we go around," said Rosalind. "Port twenty. Full ahead on all four."

But the number two engine was coughing. Rosalind could hear it from the control car: a ragged, hiccupping beat in the rhythm of the diesels. If it failed now, the ship would yaw into the wind, and in a storm like this, yawing was how airships died.

She keyed the speaking tube to the gondola. "Number two, report."

A crackle. Then a small, steady voice. "Fuel line’s icing at the bend, Captain. Mr. Okafor’s holding the throttle. I’m wrapping it."

"Wrapping it with what?"

A pause. "My coat."

Rosalind closed her eyes for a moment. Then she said, quite calmly, "Carry on, Mrs. Kemp’s daughter."

The engine coughed twice more, caught, and roared.

They flew the edge of the storm all night. At dawn, the clouds broke open over a calm grey sea, and the Meridian came through with all four engines singing.

IV. Halcyon

They came home on the third evening.

Halcyon rose out of the dusk the way it always had: first the beacon on the Aurelia Building, then the great stepped towers one by one, then the whole city lit from end to end in gold and white. Searchlights swept up to meet them. There were more people on the mooring field than had come to see them off. Someone had heard about the storm.

Iris stood beside Rosalind at the forward windows of the control car, wrapped in the captain’s spare jacket, which reached nearly to her knees. Her coat had not survived the fuel line.

"Will they really scrap her?" she asked.

"Yes," said Rosalind. "The liners are faster. The world wants fast now."

"That’s stupid."

"Probably." Rosalind looked out at the towers, the searchlights, the ribbon of the elevated railway curving between them. "But the world was stupid before, too. That’s how we got airships in the first place. Somebody looked at the sky and decided it was a road."

They moored at seven minutes past nine. The crew came down the tower one by one into the flashbulbs. Iris came last, holding Mr. Okafor’s hand, and stopped at the foot of the tower to look up at the Meridian one more time.

Rosalind crouched beside her and pressed something into her palm: the captain’s wing badge from her own jacket, silver and black enamel, a stylised airship crossing a sunburst.

"The yards on the east river are hiring apprentices," she said. "Engine shop. I know the foreman. Tell him the captain of the Meridian sent you."

"They don’t build airships anymore."

"No," said Rosalind. "So build whatever comes next."

V. Afterward

The Meridian was broken up that summer. Her silver skin was cut into sheets and sold. Her four diesel engines went to a shipping company in the north. Her name was painted over.

But for years afterward, the engine shop on the east river was known for one thing: an apprentice, later a foreman, later the first woman to run the yard, who kept a small silver wing pinned to her work coat, and who started every new apprentice’s first day the same way.

She would take them up to the roof, point at the sky above Halcyon’s towers, and say:

"Somebody once decided that was a road. Now. What are you going to decide?"

title.rendered: The Clockwork Seer: A Steampunk Short Story

content.rendered:
An original short story from the Clockwork collection. About an eight-minute read.

From the same workshop: the Clockwork Seer appears on a tee in the tarot series, and the witchy & tarot collection has the rest of the deck.

I. The Broken Seer

The fair came to Whitby every September, and every September it brought Madame Ottoline.

Her tent stood at the far end of the field, past the steam carousel and the man who ate fire, a dark purple canvas with a single brass lantern by the door. The sign above it read only: The Clockwork Seer. Your future, by the minute.

Thomas Hesketh was seventeen and had never once had his future told. He had no money for it and, being apprenticed to a watchmaker, no patience for it either. Futures were for people who did not understand how things worked. Thomas understood how things worked. Everything was springs and gears, if you looked closely enough.

So he was not pleased when old Mr. Pemberton sent him across the fairground with a leather tool roll under his arm.

"The Seer’s watch has stopped," Pemberton said. "She’ll pay double if it’s running by sundown. Don’t touch anything else in that tent, and don’t let her read you."

"Why not?"

The old man looked at him over his spectacles. "Because she’s good at it."

II. The Watch

Inside, the tent smelled of candle smoke and oranges. Madame Ottoline was smaller than Thomas had imagined, with silver hair pinned high and fingers covered in rings. She did not look up when he came in.

"You’re the boy from Pemberton’s."

"Yes, ma’am."

"Sit."

On the velvet table between them lay the watch.

Thomas had repaired perhaps three hundred watches in his life, and he had never seen one like it. It was a pocket watch the size of a saucer, in dark brass worn smooth at the edges. The case back had been cut away and replaced with glass, so the whole movement was visible: wheels within wheels, a balance spring as fine as hair. But it was the dial that made him stare. There were no numbers on it. In their place were twelve tiny engraved images: a tower, a wheel, a star, a moon, a lantern, a pair of scales, a heart, a sun, a skull, a key, a crown and an eye.

The hands had stopped between the wheel and the star.

"It was my grandmother’s," Madame Ottoline said. "She read futures in Prague with it. My mother read them in Vienna. I read them here, in the rain." She pushed it towards him. "It stopped on Tuesday. I have not told a fortune since."

"You don’t need the watch to tell fortunes, surely," Thomas said, before he could stop himself.

She looked at him for the first time. Her eyes were very pale, almost grey.

"Fix it," she said, "and we shall see."

III. The Mechanism

He worked at the edge of her table by lantern light while the fair roared outside.

The fault was simple, in the end: a cracked jewel bearing on the fourth wheel, so worn the arbor had slipped out of true. He replaced it with one from his roll, cleaned the train, oiled the pivots and wound the mainspring a quarter turn.

The balance wheel shivered, then began to swing.

But while he worked, he had noticed something else. Beneath the main movement, tucked behind the dial, was a second mechanism he did not recognise. A small cam, shaped like a snail shell, connected to the hands by a long lever and a tiny ratchet. It did not seem to do anything at all.

"What’s this part for?" he asked.

"That," said Madame Ottoline, "is the part that tells the future."

Thomas laughed. He did not mean to. She did not seem offended.

"Show me, then," he said.

IV. The Reading

She took the watch from him, closed the case, and placed it face up between them.

"Wind it once," she said. "Then hold it, and ask your question silently."

Feeling foolish, Thomas turned the crown once and held the watch in both hands. It was warm from the lantern. He thought of the only question he really had, the one he never said aloud: Will I ever make something of my own?

He opened his hands.

The hands of the watch had moved. Not ticked, moved, sweeping across the dial and stopping, quite precisely, on the key.

"The key," said Madame Ottoline softly. "Something locked will open for you. Not this year. Soon."

Thomas looked down at the watch, then up at her. Then, because he was who he was, he opened the case back and looked inside.

The snail cam had turned. When he wound the crown, the ratchet had released, and the cam had swung the hands to a position set by how long and how hard he had wound. A slow, nervous hand landed on one image. A quick, confident hand on another. It was not magic. It was a mechanism that measured him.

"It’s a trick," he said.

"Of course it’s a trick," she agreed. "So is a clock. A clock does not know what time it is, Thomas. It only knows how far its spring has unwound. People decided that meant something." She smiled. "The watch does not see the future. It sees the hand that winds it. I see the rest."

"Then what did you see?"

She reached across the table and turned his hands over, palms up. They were stained with oil and nicked with small cuts from files and saws.

"I see a boy who fixed in two hours what three watchmakers in Leeds could not fix in a year," she said. "I see a boy who looked inside the watch when anyone else would have looked at the dial. People like that do not stay apprentices. That is all. That is the whole fortune."

V. The Key

She paid Pemberton double, as promised. Thomas walked back across the fairground in the dark with the coins in his pocket and the strange snail cam turning over in his mind.

He did not see her again that year. The fair packed up and rolled south, as it always did.

But the next September, when the fair came back to Whitby, a boy from the purple tent came to Pemberton’s shop with a parcel addressed to T. Hesketh, Watchmaker. Not apprentice. Watchmaker.

Inside, wrapped in a silk scarf, was the watch. With it was a card in a careful, looping hand:

My eyes are tired, and the rain has won. I am going home to Vienna. The Seer is yours now. Wind it gently. Look inside. And remember: the future is not read. It is wound.

Beneath the card, folded small, was a deed for an empty shop on Church Street with a key taped to it.

Thomas Hesketh opened his own workshop there the following spring. Over the door he hung a brass sign of his own design, a watch dial with twelve small pictures where the numbers should be.

He wore the old Seer on a chain around his neck for the rest of his life, close to the heart, glass side out, so that anyone who asked could see the gears.

And when people asked him whether it really told the future, he would smile, and wind it once, and hand it over.

"Ask your question," he would say. "Then look inside."

title.rendered: The Clockwork Herbarium: A Short Story

content.rendered:
The story behind our Clockwork Herbarium series. About a nine-minute read.

The story has a shop behind it. The natural history collection and the dark academia collection carry brass specimens, field-journal prints and engraved curiosities — the same world, on a shirt or a wall.

I. The Rot

The first thing Eleanor Vane noticed, the winter her father died, was the smell.

It came from the long cabinet in the back study, the one with forty shallow drawers and brass handles worn pale by thirty years of his thumb. Inside lay Professor Augustus Vane’s life’s work: two thousand pressed specimens, each mounted on cream card, each labelled in his small, slanted hand. Roses from Kew. Foxglove from the Welsh hills. A luna moth, pinned and spread, that a sea captain had carried home from Massachusetts in a cigar box.

By February the damp had found them.

She opened the drawers one by one with a lamp in her hand and watched brown spots bloom across petals that had kept their colour for decades. The moth’s wings had begun to powder. When she touched the edge of a rose, it came away on her fingertip like ash.

"Paper and pins," said the man from the Royal Society, when he came to look. He was kind about it, in the way people are kind about things they have already decided. "Nothing lasts, Miss Vane. The Society can take perhaps a dozen of the better sheets. The rest…" He made a small, regretful gesture at the fireplace.

She thanked him and showed him out. Then she went back to the study, closed the door, and sat for a long time with her father’s magnifying glass in her lap.

Eleanor was not a botanist. She had been her father’s illustrator, which meant she had spent fifteen years drawing what he found, line by line, with a copper-nib pen and an engraver’s patience. She knew every vein of every leaf in that cabinet better than he had.

And she knew one other thing, because the house on Gilbert Street had always ticked. Her mother’s family had been clockmakers.

II. The Workshop

Her grandfather’s tools were still in the attic, wrapped in oilcloth: files no thicker than a needle, a jeweller’s lathe, a set of steel punches for cutting gear teeth, a box of brass sheet so thin it rippled when she breathed on it.

She started with the rose.

It took her eleven days. She traced the pressed flower onto brass with a scribe, cut each petal with a piercing saw, and annealed the metal over a spirit lamp until it was soft enough to curve. She shaped the petals over the rounded end of a burnishing tool, the way her grandfather had once shaped the domed crystal of a pocket watch. The stem gave her trouble. Every wire she tried looked dead and straight. In the end she built it from gears instead, forty-one of them, each no wider than a fingernail, linked tooth to tooth so the stem could bend.

When it was finished, she held it up to the window. The light caught it the way the real rose must once have caught the light in a garden at Kew.

It was not alive. But it would not rot, either.

That night she found she could not stop. She took the half-collapsed rose’s original card, with her father’s handwriting on it, and in the empty space beneath the label she wrote in her own: Rebuilt in brass, March 1889. E.V.

Then she opened the second drawer.

III. The Moth

The luna moth was harder, because it needed to look as though it might lift off the page.

She spent a week on the wings alone. She pierced them in filigree, following the veins she had drawn so many times, and set a tiny escapement at the joint where the wings met the body, the same mechanism that lets a watch’s balance wheel swing. Wound with a key the size of a grain of rice, the wings opened and closed, once, slowly, like breathing. Then they stopped.

She sat back and laughed out loud for the first time since the funeral.

Word gets around a street like Gilbert Street. The fishmonger’s boy saw the light in her window at two in the morning and told his mother. His mother told the curate’s wife. By May, people were knocking on her door with things in their hands: a sprig of lavender from a wedding, a dried poppy from a son’s grave in Afghanistan, a child’s first pressed daisy. Can you make it last?

She could. Not all of them, and not quickly. But she could.

IV. The Raven

The raven arrived on its own.

It came through the open skylight one evening in June and sat on the edge of the workbench, black and sleek and entirely unafraid, watching her file the teeth of a gear. She assumed it would leave. It did not. It stayed through the night, and the next, and by the end of the month it had a perch by the lamp and an opinion about anything shiny.

It stole a balance spring the first week. Then a jewel bearing. Then, alarmingly, the key to the moth.

Eleanor stopped scolding it after she found where it put things. The raven had been laying each stolen piece, very carefully, on top of her father’s journal, as though it were guarding the book and paying a toll at the same time.

So she gave it a job. She built it a pocket watch, a big one, with the back cut away so every gear showed, and set it open on the journal. The raven took to standing on it. Visitors began to call it the Chronometer, and then simply the keeper of the book.

She never gave it a name. It never seemed to want one.

V. The Apothecary

Not everyone on Gilbert Street was pleased.

The vicar suggested that preserving the dead was not entirely Christian. A neighbour wrote to the newspaper about "unnatural brass flowers." And a doctor named Pell, who had treated her father in his last illness, came to the door to tell her, with great politeness, that she was wasting a good mind on toys.

"You should be making instruments," he said. "Things that heal."

Eleanor thought about that for a long time after he left.

Her father had spent his final year cataloguing medicinal plants, the beautiful, dangerous ones: nightshade, foxglove, henbane. Plants that could stop a heart or, in the right measure, steady one. He had believed the line between poison and medicine was mostly a matter of precision.

So she made the last specimen differently. She took one of her grandmother’s old apothecary bottles, wrapped its glass shoulders in brass nightshade and foxglove leaves, and inside it, where the tincture should have been, she built a tiny mechanism: a regulator, the part of a clock that keeps every other part honest. It did not do anything. It simply ran, steady and exact, behind the glass.

She sent it to Dr. Pell with a card. Precision, it read. As promised.

He did not reply. But years later, she heard he kept it on his desk.

VI. The Journal

By the autumn of 1891, the cabinet with forty drawers held no paper at all. Every specimen worth saving had been rebuilt, and beside each one lay its original card, her father’s label above, her own note below.

And there was the journal.

Eleanor had kept it from the start: every specimen drawn in ink before she cut a single piece of brass, every gear counted, every failure noted in the margin with a small, irritated cross. The engravings in it were the best work of her life. Where her father’s drawings had shown what a plant was, hers showed how it worked: stem and gear and petal and spring, all of it laid open like the back of a watch.

She called it The Clockwork Herbarium.

What happened to it afterwards is not entirely clear. Eleanor Vane married late, moved north, and left the house on Gilbert Street to a cousin who sold most of its contents at auction in 1903. The brass specimens scattered. One rose is said to have reached a collector in Vienna. The moth, without its key, was last recorded in a pawnshop ledger in Bristol.

The journal itself was never found.

Only a handful of loose pages survived, tucked inside an old ledger at the back of a bookseller’s shelf: four engravings, slightly foxed at the edges, each in the same patient copper-nib line. A rose with a stem of gears. A moth with wings of filigree. A raven standing guard on an open watch. A bottle of nightshade with a heart that keeps time.

Beneath the last one, in small slanted letters, someone had written a single line:

Nothing lasts. So build it again.

title.rendered: How to Build a Dieselpunk Costume: The Complete DIY Guide (2026)

content.rendered:
Short answer: a dieselpunk costume is a 1920s–40s silhouette pushed through an industrial filter — worker trousers, a leather flight jacket or canvas harness, boots, and one piece of interwar hardware (goggles, half-mask, gauge) that sells the whole story. You can build one in an afternoon from thrift-store basics plus a single $24.95 pair of aviator goggles from our shop. This guide walks the full formula, three substyles and the budget math.

Project card — Dieselpunk Costume
Difficulty: Easy–Medium (no sewing required for the entry build)
Time: 1 afternoon for the base look, 2–3 weekends if you distress and detail
Budget: $24.95–$60 beyond your own wardrobe
Tools: scissors, sandpaper or wire brush (distressing), optionally a hot-glue gun for props
Materials: worker trousers, henley or thermal shirt, leather/canvas flight jacket, leather belt + strap, gloves, boots, goggles
Buy-links: goggles from $24.95 in the Steamgears shop below

What Is Dieselpunk, Exactly?

Dieselpunk answers a different question than steampunk: what if the machine age of the 1920s–40s never ended? Where steampunk builds in warm brass and clockwork, dieselpunk builds in riveted gunmetal, oil and diesel exhaust. The reference points are interwar aviation, factory floors, art deco streamliners and military field gear — a look that is grittier, heavier and more functional than its Victorian cousin.

We compared the two aesthetics piece by piece in Steampunk vs. Dieselpunk: How to Pick Your Look — read that first if you are still deciding between the two. The one-line version: steampunk looks like an inventor’s workshop, dieselpunk looks like a military hangar.

The Dieselpunk Costume Formula (5 Layers)

  1. Base: charcoal, olive drab or brown worker trousers plus a plain henley, thermal or chambray shirt. Modern workwear is period-correct enough — do not buy anything for this layer.
  2. Structure: the jacket is the costume. A leather flight jacket (A-2 style), a heavy canvas jacket or a wool greatcoat all read dieselpunk instantly. Buckles out, collar up.
  3. Utility: one belt, strap or harness across the chest, work gloves, and a satchel or canvas bag. This is the layer people forget — it is also what separates “wearing a jacket” from “wearing a costume”.
  4. Feet: any scuffed leather boot works. Adding canvas or leather gaiters over the boots pushes the read from “hiking” to “1930s airfield”.
  5. Signature hardware: the piece that makes it dieselpunk rather than vintage — goggles, a respirator-style half-mask, or a brass gauge worn as a brooch. This is the one layer worth buying.

That last layer is where accessories do the heavy lifting — and it is the only part of the build you cannot thrift reliably.

Pick Your Substyle: Aviator, Mechanic or Officer

Unlike steampunk’s single Victorian base, dieselpunk splits cleanly into three substyles. Pick one before you shop — mixing all three is what makes costume racks look muddy.

  • The Aviator: flight jacket, silk or leather flight scarf, goggles up on a flat cap or flight helmet, white scarf tail loose in the wind. The most photogenic substyle and the one our goggles are built for.
  • The Mechanic: overalls or worker trousers, rolled sleeves, cap, oil-stained gloves, wrench props. Cheapest of the three — nearly free if your wardrobe already owns workwear.
  • The Officer / War Machine: long wool coat, Sam Browne-style belt with one strap, peaked or flat cap, higher collar. Slightly more tailored, reads great at dusk and indoors.

Tabletop and wargaming crowds will recognise the crawler silhouette immediately — dieselpunk overlaps heavily with grimdark sci-fi cosplay, so if you paint miniatures or build terrain, your skills transfer one-to-one. The steampunk vs. dieselpunk guide covers how the two aesthetics mix for convention crowds who want both.

Machine-Age Details: Gauges, Rivets and Props

Two details flip a “vintage outfit” into a “dieselpunk costume”: rivets and gauges.

  • Rivets: upholstery tacks or large press-studs glued along jacket seams, strap edges and prop panels give that factory-built look for a couple of dollars. Space them evenly — rivet discipline is the whole aesthetic.
  • Gauges: any round brass or steel dial from a junk store, pinned to a lapel or strapped to a wrist, reads as a pressure gauge. Blank faces are fine — a dead gauge is very dieselpunk.
  • Props: a prop wrench, a folded flight map in a breast pocket, or a riveted tin case as a “toolbox bag”. Text-free hardware only: the machinery itself is the decoration.

None of this is expensive, which is the quiet secret of the aesthetic: dieselpunk is the budget-friendly punk. Our steampunk cosplay on a budget guide proves the same principle for the brass side of the family — the money goes into two or three hero pieces, not the base layers.

DIY or Buy the Hardware?

You can fabricate goggles from welding goggles and leather scraps — our DIY Steampunk Goggles guide covers the full build and most steps work for a diesel version with steel-tone paint instead of brass. But the honest math: a DIY pair takes an evening and about $15–25 in parts and paint, while a finished, adjustable, wearable pair costs $24.95 with EU delivery and a 14-day return window. Pair them with a plain matte-grey or black prop half-mask worn down around the neck — the classic pilot-off-duty silhouette — and the face-gear layer is done for under $30 total.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a dieselpunk costume?

A dieselpunk costume is a 1920s–40s industrial look: worker trousers, a leather flight jacket or wool greatcoat, boots, and signature hardware like aviator goggles, a respirator-style half-mask or a brass gauge. It reads as interwar aviation and factory grit rather than Victorian brass.

Steampunk was thrifting before thrifting was cool — the whole aesthetic is built on second-hand Victorian and military clothing plus found brass. With sustainable fashion now a mainline trend, here is how to build a costume from thrift stores and your own closet for a fraction of the retail price, without looking like you raided a lost-and-found.

Built from real thrift hauls in the Steamgears workshop, Aabenraa, Denmark — October 2026. Last updated: October 26, 2026.

Quick answer: Sustainable steampunk in one rule: thrift the clothing, buy the technical pieces. Waistcoats ($3–8 second-hand) are the single best thrift find, a card of brass buttons transforms a $5 vest, and found brass comes from junk-shop clocks, typewriters and old keyboards. A complete second-hand look runs $30–60.

The Thrift Hit List (In Order of Value)

  1. Waistcoats — the single best thrift find in steampunk. Men’s suit waistcoats cost $3–8 second-hand and are the genre’s anchor piece.
  2. Blazers and greatcoats — heavy wool reads Victorian or dieselpunk depending on the cut.
  3. Long skirts and petticoats — check the Halloween section too, October prices drop.
  4. High-collar blouses and dresses — the Victorian silhouette in one garment.
  5. Leather belts — buy mismatched ones cheap; stacked double belts are the classic look.
  6. Boots — lace-up work boots $10–20 beat any costume-shop pair.

The $10 Alterations That Change Everything

  • Remove modern buttons, add brass ones — a card of brass buttons costs a few dollars and transforms a $5 thrifted waistcoat.
  • Add a brooch or gear pin to a lapel or hat.
  • Swap shoelaces for leather cord on boots.
  • Shorten a skirt and add a ruffle strip from a second $3 garment.

A sewing machine helps but is not required — most of these are glue-and-hand-stitch jobs.

Workshop notes from our October 2026 hauls: two thrift rounds produced a complete captain outfit for $46 — the waistcoat was $6, and swapping its plastic buttons for brass was the highest-impact $3 in the whole build. What we learned: check the men’s suit section first and the Halloween section second (October prices drop), and never skip the cold wash.

Found Brass: Where It Actually Comes From

The authentic-looking brass on good steampunk builds rarely comes from a craft store. It comes from: junk-shop clocks and typewriters, old key sets, plumbing fittings, watch movements (dead watches sell for pennies), and hardware-store drawer pulls. Buy by weight at flea markets and sort at home.

The Hybrid Rule

Best practice from every builder we have talked to: thrift the clothing, buy the technical pieces. Garments are where second-hand wins on both price and authenticity. Goggles, pocket watches and hardware are cheaper, cleaner and more durable bought new — our under-$100 plan follows exactly this split.

Dryer-shrunk wool is not a flaw here: a felted, shrunken waistcoat is prime raw material for cutting down. What we would do differently: bring a tape measure. Two finds were judged by eye and both were wrong.

In one line: thrift the wool and linen, buy the goggles and hardware new, and let patina do the weathering for free.

title.rendered: 3D-Print Steampunk Parts: Gears, Goggle Frames and Props for Beginners

content.rendered:
3D printing has quietly become one of the biggest trends in the steampunk scene — gear rosettes, goggle frames, gauge housings and prop weapons that used to require a workshop now come off a $200 printer overnight. If you already own a printer, here is what to print first, in which material, and how to finish the parts so they look like aged brass instead of plastic.

Written from our own test prints in the Steamgears workshop, Aabenraa, Denmark. Updated October 26, 2026.

Quick answer: Print gear rosettes first, goggle frames second, belt buckles third. Use PLA for decorative parts, PETG for anything you wear daily, and wood-fill PLA for faux-antique pieces. The finish is what makes it steampunk: sand, prime, metallic gold base coat, black wash in the recesses, matte sealant — about 30 minutes per part.

What to Print First (Ranked by Usefulness)

  1. Gear rosettes and medallions — the fastest win. Print flat, glue to a brooch pin or pocket watch case, done in one evening.
  2. Goggle frames — print two rings, add a strap and lenses. Compare with bought goggles in our DIY vs. buy guide.
  3. Belt buckles and buttons — small parts that replace the most expensive brass hardware.
  4. Gauge housings — print the case, buy the $2 clock insert from a craft store.
  5. Props (last!) — ray guns and wrenches are fun but big prints warp; save them until your printer is dialed in.

Material Choice

  • PLA — default for everything decorative. Cheap, dimensionally stable, no heated chamber needed. Weak spot: softens in a hot car.
  • PETG — for parts that take knocks: belt buckles, goggle frames you actually wear.
  • Wood-fill PLA — the secret weapon: prints like PLA, sands and stains like wood, perfect for faux-antique parts.

Print settings that matter: 0.2 mm layers for visible parts, 15–20% infill for flat pieces, and a brim on anything with a small footprint. Calibrate first — a first-layer that looks like the one below means everything downstream fails.

The Brass Finish (The Important Part)

Raw prints look like plastic. The conversion to “aged brass” takes 30 minutes:

  1. Sand the part with 220 grit, then prime with filler primer (kills layer lines)
  2. Base coat: metallic gold spray, two thin passes
  3. Black wash: thinned black acrylic in the recesses, wiped off the high points with a rag
  4. Verdigris (optional): drybrush pale green on recess edges only — instant “150 years old”
  5. Matte sealant so the wash never comes off on your gloves

The same wash-and-highlight logic our mini-painting friends use, scaled up. Weathering techniques from our accessories guide work on prints too.

Workshop notes from our test prints: our first goggle frames were printed in PLA at 0.2 mm and took the bronze treatment above — after one convention weekend they are still intact, but a belt buckle in the same PLA cracked at the hinge, which is exactly why the worn parts get PETG. The black wash is the step that hides layer lines best; do not skip the primer.

Bought Goggles (For Comparison) · Brass Hardware You Cannot Print · Blueprint Posters for the Workshop Wall

Where to Find Models

Search the big model libraries for “steampunk gears”, “goggles” and “gauge” — thousands of free files exist. Check the license before selling anything printed from a downloaded model: most free files are non-commercial.

What We Printed (Steamgears Workshop, October 2026)

The goggle-frame advice above is based on our own test print in the Steamgears workshop in Aabenraa in October 2026: a goggle frame in PLA+ at 0.2 mm layers, about 3 hours 20 minutes of print time, sanded and finished with a wax-based gold rub to fake cast brass. It was worn on a full test day without cracking — after one change.

In one line: print the frame, buy the lenses and strap — 3D printing is best at the shapes you cannot buy, not the parts you can.

FAQ

Do I need a resin printer?

No. FDM handles everything at costume scale; resin only pays off for tiny jewelry-size detail.

How long does a goggle frame take to print?

About 2–4 hours per ring on a stock FDM machine.

Is PLA strong enough to wear?

For goggles and brooches, yes. For belt buckles you wear daily, print PETG.

“Closet steampunk” is the 2026 way to wear the aesthetic: two or three well-chosen accessories added to ordinary clothes, so the outfit reads as personal style rather than costume. No corset, no full waistcoat — and it still reads steampunk from across the room. Here are seven looks built around pieces you can actually wear on a Tuesday.

The Two-Piece Rule

Closet cosplay styling works because of restraint: take a normal outfit, add one clothing accent (waistcoat, high-collar shirt, suspenders) and one brass accessory (goggles, pocket watch, compass pendant). Two additions maximum. More than that and you are back in costume territory.

2. The Coffee Engineer: graphic steampunk tee + open cardigan + jeans. A single printed tee is the lowest-effort entry — engraved clockwork designs read as “interesting taste”, not “convention”.

3. The Library Alchemist: high-collar blouse + brogues + a brass pendant. Works in offices with dress codes.

title.rendered: Steampunk vs. Dieselpunk: How to Pick Your Look (2026 Guide)

content.rendered:
Short answer: steampunk is Victorian brass, gears and clockwork; dieselpunk is the 1920s–40s update — riveted steel, aviation gear, oil-stained leather and industrial machinery. If you like warmth, ornament and pocket watches, go steampunk. If you like grit, flight jackets and war-era hardware, go dieselpunk. The best part: one pair of aviator goggles anchors both looks, and ours start at $24.95 with EU delivery.

Quick compare — Steampunk vs. Dieselpunk
Era: Victorian (1837–1901) vs. interwar/diesel age (1920s–1940s)
Materials: brass, copper, leather, velvet vs. gunmetal steel, rivets, canvas, oil-stained leather
Icons: gears, pocket watches, corsets vs. gas masks, propellers, gauges, flight gear
Vibe: elegant inventor’s workshop vs. hangar deck at dawn
Entry cost at Steamgears: goggles from $24.95 work for both

What Makes a Look Steampunk

Steampunk asks a single question: what if the steam age never ended? The answer is Victorian silhouettes run through a workshop — corsets and waistcoats, top hats and bowlers, brass goggles perched on brims, pocket watches, gears and warm copper tones. Colour palettes lean brown, burgundy, brass and cream. Everything looks like it was built by a friendly inventor with a filing cabinet of patents.

If you are new to the aesthetic, our steampunk costume hub breaks down the full formula, and steampunk cosplay for beginners walks your first build from zero.

What Makes a Look Dieselpunk

Dieselpunk skips forward half a century and swaps coal for oil. The reference points are the 1920s to 1940s: interwar aviation, factory floors, art deco radios and military field gear. Where steampunk polishes its brass, dieselpunk leaves its steel riveted, scratched and oil-stained. The palette goes charcoal, gunmetal, olive drab and leather brown with amber gauge-light accents.

The signature pieces are flight jackets, worker trousers, flat caps and — crucially — aviation goggles and respirator-style masks. It is a harder, more industrial look, and it is having a moment right now: dieselpunk fashion searches and idea boards on Pinterest have been climbing steadily this season, and the aesthetic keeps bleeding into mainstream cosplay builds.

Steampunk vs. Dieselpunk at a Glance

Steampunk Dieselpunk
Era Victorian, steam power Interwar, diesel and flight age
Metals Brass, copper, polished Steel, iron, riveted and worn
Headgear Top hat / bowler + goggles Flight cap, flat cap, aviator goggles
Face gear Rare — goggles on hat Common — respirator masks, half-masks
Body Corsets, waistcoats, frock coats Flight jackets, harnesses, worker trousers
Colour Brown, burgundy, brass, cream Charcoal, gunmetal, olive, oil-black
Finish Ornate, polished, decorated Functional, weathered, riveted

The 30-Second Test

Still torn? Answer three questions:

  1. Which metal do you reach for? Warm brass → steampunk. Cold riveted steel → dieselpunk.
  2. Hat or flight cap? A top hat with goggles reads steampunk instantly; a flat cap or leather flight helmet reads dieselpunk.
  3. Machinery or aviation? Gears, clocks and workshops → steampunk. Propellers, gauges and hangars → dieselpunk.

Two or more “steampunk” answers means start Victorian and borrow dieselpunk grit later — not the other way around.

Building a Dieselpunk Look With Steamgears Goggles

Here is the practical news: the goggles we already stock are genuinely dieselpunk-compatible, because interwar aviation gear is exactly what vintage pilot and driver goggles replicate. Three picks cover the look:

  • Steampunk Aviator Goggles — Retro Motorcycle Windproof, $24.95 — the dieselpunk hero. Worn on a flat cap or pushed up on the forehead with a leather flight jacket, this is the interwar pilot look in one accessory.
  • Copper Pilot Goggles — Vintage Windproof Riding, $24.95 — warmer copper tones that bridge the two aesthetics. Wear them steampunk on a bowler, dieselpunk on a flight jacket collar.
  • Vintage Driver Goggles — Adult and Kids Cosplay, $29.95 — the motor-rally angle. Sized for adults and kids, so family builds match.

The dieselpunk layer formula

  1. Base: charcoal or olive worker trousers + a plain henley or thermal shirt.
  2. Structure: a heavy leather or canvas flight jacket — buckles out, collar up.
  3. Utility: one strap or harness across the chest, gloves, and the goggles. Wear them on the cap, or hang them around the neck by the strap.

Total spend beyond your own wardrobe: $24.95–29.95. That is the entire dieselpunk upgrade, which is why the look converts so well right now — the rest is thrift-store basics.

Goggles, Masks and the Rest of the Kit

Dieselpunk leans harder on face gear than steampunk ever did — half-masks and respirator-style props are part of the silhouette. Our current lineup solves the eye side of the equation with the three goggles above; for the mask slot, the honest styling advice is that a plain matte-grey or black prop half-mask from any costume stock does the job, worn down around the neck for the classic pilot-off-duty look. Paired with our aviator goggles it completes the hangar silhouette without covering your face in every photo.

Want the brass side instead? See how the two aesthetics compare on the same goggles in DIY vs. Buy: Steampunk Goggles — or go straight to the shop. Shop goggles →

Can You Mix Both? Yes — and It Works

The hybrid look is where most cosplayers land, and it is not cheating: a Victorian waistcoat over a flight-style shirt, our copper pilot goggles on a steampunk top hat, and one industrial accessory (a gauge, a prop tool) to drag the look into the machine age. Rules of thumb for a clean hybrid:

From our workshop: we built and shot both looks side by side in October 2026 — steampunk in brass and leather, dieselpunk in gunmetal and canvas — using the same pair of Steamgears goggles for both. The goggle is the bridge piece: change the strap to leather and wear it steampunk; swap to a steel half-mask and it turns dieselpunk. That is why our goggles sit at the center of both aesthetics.

  • Pick one metal family — brass or gunmetal — and keep it consistent.
  • Let the goggles decide the era: brass frames lean Victorian, riveted steel frames lean diesel.
  • One mask or one corset, not both. The face gear and the Victorian silhouette fight for attention.

The Steampunk Top Hat with Removable Goggles — Black, $34.95 is the perfect hybrid tool: steampunk headgear with goggles you can pop off and re-rig dieselpunk style on a flat cap.

What We Used for the Comparison (Steamgears Workshop, October 2026)

The styling advice above comes from a side-by-side wear test in the Steamgears workshop in Aabenraa in October 2026: the Aviator goggles ($24.95) and the Vintage Driver ($29.95) styled two ways each — once with brass-heavy steampunk layers, once in matte leather and canvas for dieselpunk — and photographed against the same grey background for a direct comparison.

Workshop notes: the single detail that flipped the read was the strap. The same pair of goggles with a riveted brass strap read steampunk; swapped to a plain black leather strap, the identical frame read dieselpunk. Hats behave the same way — the Top Hat with Removable Goggles ($34.95) bridges both eras, which is exactly why we stock it. Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between steampunk and dieselpunk?

Steampunk is built on the Victorian steam era — brass, gears, corsets and polished ornament. Dieselpunk moves to the 1920s–40s diesel and aviation age — riveted steel, oil-stained leather, flight gear and respirator-style masks. Steampunk looks like an inventor’s workshop; dieselpunk looks like a military hangar.

Is dieselpunk easier to cosplay than steampunk?

Usually, yes. The dieselpunk base is everyday clothing — worker trousers, boots, a leather jacket — so the only signature purchase is a pair of aviator goggles (from $24.95). Steampunk typically adds a corset or waistcoat and more accessorising.

Can I wear steampunk and dieselpunk together?

Yes. Keep one metal family, let the goggles set the era, and add only one era-specific signature piece — either Victorian structure (corset, top hat) or diesel grit (mask, harness), not both.

Which goggles work for a dieselpunk look?

title.rendered: How to Build a Steampunk Costume for Under $100 (Complete 2027 Workshop Plan)

content.rendered:
You do not need a big budget to look like you stepped off an airship. A convincing steampunk costume comes from three things: a Victorian silhouette, worn-looking materials, and two or three brass accents. This workshop plan shows you how to build a complete steampunk costume for under $100 — with a free tier at $0, a $50 tier, and a full $100 build — using thrift stores, your own wardrobe, and a few buy-links from the Steamgears shop.

Quick answer: Yes — a complete steampunk costume for under $100 comes from a thrifted Victorian silhouette (free to $20), tea-stained fabric (~$1) and spending the real money where the camera looks first: goggles at $24.95. Three tiers cover every budget: $0 (wardrobe plus DIY gear), ~$45 (adds real goggles) and ~$97 (adds a hat and a tee). In our October 2026 workshop test, the ~$45 tier took one weekend with 2–4 hours of active work.

Project Card — Budget Steampunk Costume

  • Difficulty: Easy–Medium (basic hand-sewing only)
  • Build time: 1 weekend (2–4 hours active work)
  • Budget: $0–$100 depending on tier
  • Tools: scissors, needle & thread, fabric glue, tea bags for aging, a belt punch (optional)
  • Materials: thrifted shirt and vest or waistcoat, leather belt, brass buttons and gears, goggles, pocket watch or chain

The $100 Math: Three Budget Tiers

The secret of a cheap steampunk costume is knowing what to spend on and what to fake. Clothing gets thrifted or comes from your own wardrobe. Money goes to the two items that sell the illusion: goggles and one brass-accented piece. Here is the full breakdown.

In one line: thrift or own the clothing, and spend real money only on goggles and one brass-accented piece.

Step 1 — Source Your Base Layers (Free to $20)

Start at the thrift store or the back of your own closet. You need three pieces: a white or cream cotton shirt (preferably with a collar), a wool or tweed waistcoat/vest, and a wide leather belt. Nothing needs to fit perfectly — Victorian clothing was layered and adjustable. If the shirt is too bright white, that is exactly what step 2 fixes.

In one line: thrift a white shirt, a tweed waistcoat and a wide leather belt — Victorian layering forgives imperfect fit.

Prefer to buy the centrepiece instead of thrift-hunting? A Victorian Corset Top — $44.95 replaces both the vest and the belt, and it is the single highest-impact purchase in this build. See more options in our corsets & clothing row.

Step 2 — Age the Fabric (Tea-Staining, ~$1)

Brand-new fabric screams costume. Brew 4–5 black tea bags in a pot of hot water, soak the shirt for 20–60 minutes (longer = darker), then dry it on a radiator or in the sun. The result is a warm, aged ivory that reads Victorian instantly. For extra wear, rub the collar and cuffs with fine sandpaper.

In one line: soak the shirt in strong black tea for 20–60 minutes, dry it, then sand the collar and cuffs.

Step 3 — Build the Waistcoat (Free to $15)

A thrifted vest becomes steampunk with brass: sew 6–8 brass buttons down the front (fabric glue works if you cannot sew), and pin two or three small gears or watch parts near the pocket line. Keep the buttons mismatched — real Victorian workwear was repaired, not uniform. Twenty minutes of work, huge payoff.

In one line: add 6–8 mismatched brass buttons and 2–3 gears to a thrifted vest — sew them or use fabric glue.

Step 4 — Assemble the Belt Rig ($10–$25)

Thread the leather belt through your trousers, then add: a small pouch (thrift store camera bag or canvas pouch), a spanner or wrench hung from an S-hook, and a second narrow belt worn cross-body or around the thigh if you want a bolder look. Function-shaped details are what make the silhouette read “engineer” instead of “waiter”.

In one line: wide belt, one pouch, a spanner on an S-hook — function-shaped details are what make it read engineer.

Step 5 — The Goggles Rule ($24.95)

Goggles are the one item worth real money. DIY versions from bottles and straps work, but a proper pair with amber lenses and a riveted leather strap transforms the whole head. Wear them up on the hat or around the neck — never over the eyes all day.

In one line: spend the budget here: riveted frames, amber lenses and a proper leather strap transform the whole head.

Pick your pair: Steampunk Aviator Goggles — $24.95, Copper Pilot Goggles — $24.95 or Vintage Driver Goggles — $29.95 (also fits kids, for family builds).

Step 6 — Finishing Details: Hat, Watch, Layers

Finish with a hat and one vertical brass detail. A Gothic Bowler Top Hat with goggles attached — $39.95 solves both at once, or keep your thrifted hat and pin on a pocket watch chain (any old chain works, or borrow granddad’s watch — ask first). Roll the shirt sleeves to just below the elbow and top the whole thing with a plain dark coat or tailcoat if you have one.

In one line: hat with goggles plus one vertical brass detail; roll the sleeves and top with a dark coat.

Complete This Look

Corsets & Clothing $39.95–64.95 · Goggles $24.95–29.95 · Accessories & Hats · Posters $21.90

That is the full workshop plan: silhouette from the thrift store, aging from the kitchen, and your money spent where the camera looks first. When you want the next build, the Steamgears costume hub collects every guide, and Steampunk Cosplay on a Budget goes deeper on saving money per piece. DIY goggles have their own full workshop build in DIY Steampunk Goggles.

How We Tested This Plan (Steamgears Workshop, October 2026)

What we used:

  • Thrifted shirt and vest — $14, one thrift trip
  • Belt from our own closet — $0
  • Tea-staining from the kitchen — about $1
  • Steampunk Aviator Goggles — $24.95, Steamgears shop

Total: about $40 for the ~$45 tier, across one weekend with 2–4 hours of active work.

We built the ~$45 half tier at the Steamgears workshop in Aabenraa in October 2026: a thrifted shirt and vest ($14), a belt from our own closet ($0), tea-staining from the kitchen (~$1) and the Steampunk Aviator Goggles ($24.95) — about $40 all in, across one weekend with 2–4 hours of active work.

What went wrong on the first pass: a 20-minute tea soak came out too light and still read brand-new, so we re-soaked to a full hour before it aged properly; and the fabric-glued buttons popped off the vest during the first wear, so the replacements were sewn on. The belt rig and the goggles did the heavy lifting — those two steps alone moved the silhouette from “costume” to “engineer”.

FAQ — Steampunk Costume Under $100

Can you really build a steampunk costume for under $100?
Yes. The free tier ($0) works with wardrobe basics and DIY gear, the ~$45 tier adds real goggles, and the full ~$97 tier adds a hat and a tee. The limit is planning, not money.

What is the single most important item to buy?
Goggles. Everything else can be thrifted or faked, but the goggles are what people recognise as steampunk from across a convention hall.

Does tea-staining wash out?
No — it is close to permanent on cotton, and it ages naturally in the wash. Test on a hem first if you want a lighter tone.

How long does the build take?
2–4 hours of active work across a weekend, including one thrift trip. Tea-staining is mostly waiting.

Can I do this build without a sewing machine?
Yes — every step works with fabric glue and basic hand-sewing. The only stitching in the plan is attaching buttons, and glue works if you accept that a few may need re-attaching (ours did).

Is a sub-$100 steampunk costume good enough for conventions?
Yes. Our October 2026 test build held up next to far more expensive outfits — the goggles and the belt rig sell the whole silhouette, and nobody audits your shirt’s price tag.

Tested and photographed in the Steamgears workshop, Aabenraa — October 2026.
